Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

issues.item: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'Hard to Recall Deliberately' conflicts with 'Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.' Deliberate retrieval difficulty and very easy verbal access are opposing states and are hard to reconcile as describing the same patient at the same time, especially alongside 'Overwhelm on Recall,' which implies traumatic recall is effortful and dysregulating rather than easy to discuss.

issues.item: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' directly conflicts with 'When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop.' At this severity level and with strong Trigger↔Memory and Memory→Threat links, these two memory items describe opposing levels of accessibility/distress and are hard to reconcile as the same current presentation.

issues.item: Triggers: Authority Commands: Being given orders or instructions
issues.explanation: The trigger set is hard to reconcile with stalking as the index trauma: 'authority commands' and especially 'bicycle' do not show an evident clinical link to the reported trauma, and the profile provides no memory or appraisal content that would make these idiosyncratic triggers understandable.

Threat items emphasize broad interpersonal attack and generic danger vigilance (loud sounds, scanning exits, watching others for harm), which fits assault/combat/fire trauma better than stalking. For stalking, one would expect threat focused more on being followed, approached, monitored, contacted, or found by the perpetrator.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
issues.explanation: 'I am a weak person' sits awkwardly with this profile and occupation unless supported by appraisal content about failure to protect oneself or family; here the other appraisals center on permanent damage and fear of going crazy, so the weakness item feels less coherent with the stalking-specific formulation than those items.

vignette:
Karim's Vigil

Karim had been a firefighter for twelve years, and in that time he had learned to move through crisis with the steadiness of someone trained to trust his own reflexes. At thirty-seven, married to Yasmin for nine years, he had built a life that felt solid—the kind of life his parents, who had emigrated from Lebanon before he was born, had worked hard to make possible for him. But the man who showed up to the firehouse now was not the same one who had left it on a Tuesday morning in early March.

The stalking had begun without announcement. Karim first noticed the bicycle in early February—a man he didn't recognize, riding slowly past his house on Maple Street at odd hours. The man never approached, never spoke. He simply appeared: at the corner when Karim left for work, parked outside the station one afternoon, waiting on the sidewalk when Karim and Yasmin returned from the market. When Karim tried to speak to him, the man would cycle away quickly, only to reappear the next day. Karim had called the police, filed reports, changed his route home. Nothing stopped it. The man's face—lean, expressionless, eyes that seemed to catalogue Karim's movements—had burned itself into Karim's mind with the intensity of a threat he could see but not fully understand or control.

Then, on that Tuesday in March, the man had been waiting outside the station at dawn. When Karim stepped outside to begin his shift, the man stood directly in his path, close enough that Karim could see the detail of his worn jacket. "I know where you live," the man had said quietly. "I know where your wife goes." Karim had moved toward him, but the man had melted backward into the pre-dawn darkness, and by the time Karim reached the street, he was gone. The police arrested him three days later after Yasmin spotted him outside their bedroom window. The man was charged; he was held. But something in Karim had not been arrested with him.

In the weeks that followed, Karim's body became a instrument of vigilance. He could not enter a room without cataloguing its exits—the door to the kitchen, the window in the break room, the side entrance at the station. His colleagues had begun to notice. During calls, he was sharp, reliable, but back at the station, something had shifted. He would sit in the common area with his back to the wall, watching the faces of the firefighters around him, searching for the subtle signs of threat he had learned to read in the stalker's blank expression. When a truck rumbled past the station or a siren wailed in the distance, his entire body would tense. Loud, unexpected sounds made his heart race in a way that embarrassed him—a grown man, trained for emergencies, jumping at noise.

What frightened Karim most was the conviction that had settled into his chest: that he had become weak. A weak man would have been followed. A weak man would be afraid now. He had come to believe that the stalking had exposed something true about him, something permanent. He was not the steady, reliable person he had always thought he was. The evidence was in how he scanned rooms, in how he could not sleep without checking the locks twice, in how the sight of a bicycle—any bicycle, ridden by anyone—could send him into a state of panic so overwhelming that he had to step away from whatever he was doing and breathe until the world stopped spinning.

Yasmin had suggested, gently, that he talk to someone. She had noticed that he was withdrawing, that he had stopped attending the community dinners they used to enjoy, that he flinched when she touched him unexpectedly. He had resisted at first. But three weeks ago, when he found himself unable to describe to his captain why he had reacted so violently to a fellow firefighter's joke about being followed, when the memory had crashed over him without warning and left him standing in the apparatus bay unable to speak, unable to articulate what was happening inside him, he had finally called. Now, sitting in a therapist's office, Karim was trying to find the words for what it meant to have been changed by someone else's gaze, and to believe that the change was permanent.
